title: Approximability estimate of balanced group convolution: the K(1-1/N)^3 bound for the optimal intergroup error
author: Youngkyu Lee, Jongho Park, Chang-Ock Lee
work: Balanced Group Convolution: An Improved Group Convolution Based on Approximability Estimates
difficulty_reason: Supplying the article's own prerequisites - the block matrix form of a standard convolution, the group convolution, the definition of the balanced group convolution with its intergroup mean, the approximability functional, Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, the Young-type inequality of Lemma 3.3 and the K/n improvement of Lemma 3.4, both with complete proofs, and the whole of Theorem 3.5 with its proof - still leaves a source-local assembly that is not a qualification exercise. The counted proof has to build the balancing term from the intergroup mean, verify that the balanced group convolution reproduces the standard convolution up to the group-diagonal part, decompose the residual into one summand per group of the form \|\sum_{l != k} \bW^{kl} (\bx^l - \bar{\bx})\|^2, re-run the group-convolution estimate of Theorem 3.5 with the centred channels \bx^l - \bar{\bx} in place of the channels \bx^l (using that the independence of the input coordinates was never used there), and then convert the centred norm through the exact identity \bbE[\|\bar{\bx}\|^2] = N^{-2}\bbE[\|\bx\|^2] + ((N-1)/N)\|\bbE[\bx^1]\|^2 into the extra (1-1/N) factor, carrying the two assumption regimes C_{n,N,k} = K and C_{n,N,k} = K/(n-n/N) through to the two constants K(1-1/N)^3 and (K/n)(1-1/N)^2. Producing an original approximability guarantee of this shape, rather than evaluating a textbook inequality, places the unit beyond ordinary PhD qualifying examinations in numerical analysis and learning theory.
